- Johanna L Höög<sup>1</sup> †
- Sylvain Lacomble<sup>1</sup>
- Eileen T O’Toole<sup>2</sup>
- Andreas Hoenger<sup>2</sup>
- J Richard McIntosh<sup>2</sup>
- Keith Gull<sup>1</sup>

## Abstract

10.7554/eLife.01479.001 Defects in flagella growth are related to a number of human diseases. Central to flagellar growth is the organization of microtubules that polymerize from basal bodies to form the axoneme, which consists of hundreds of proteins. Flagella exist in all eukaryotic phyla, but neither the mechanism by which flagella grow nor the conservation of this process in evolution are known. Here, we study how protein complexes assemble onto the growing axoneme tip using (cryo) electron tomography. In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii microtubules and associated proteins are added simultaneously. However, in Trypanosoma brucei , disorganized arrays of microtubules are arranged into the axoneme structure by the later addition of preformed protein complexes. Post assembly, the T. brucei transition zone alters structure and its association with the central pair loosens. We conclude that there are multiple ways to form a flagellum and that species-specific structural knowledge is critical before evaluating flagellar defects. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.7554/eLife.01479.001

## Introduction

Most vertebrate cells have a cilium or flagellum (the terms are used here interchangeable). It is a thin, microtubule-containing, membrane-covered extension on the surface of the cell, which may generate cell motility and/or act as a sensory and signaling organelle. Defects in cilia and flagella can cause severe human diseases for example skeletal deformations, polycystic kidney disease, infertility, situs invertus, blindness, obesity, and even cancer (Escudier et al., 2009; Chandok, 2012; Huber and Cormier-Daire, 2012; Li et al., 2012). A collective name for these conditions is the ‘ciliopathies’ (Fliegauf et al., 2007). Some ciliopathies, such as primary ciliary dyskinesia, are diagnosed by ultrastructural investigations of cilia that should be motile (Chandok, 2012; Chilvers et al., 2003; Escudier et al., 2009; Huber and Cormier-Daire, 2012; Li et al., 2012; O’Toole et al., 2012). However, the ultrastructural pathology of many ciliopathies remains unknown.

Each flagellum consists of ∼1000 different proteins (

In most multicellular organisms, the cilium is produced after the cell has exited the cell cycle, but in many protozoan flagellates, new flagella must be built to maintain motility in daughter cells (Ginger et al., 2008; Dawson and House, 2010). Flagellar elongation occurs by addition of protein subunits at the axoneme’s distal end (Rosenbaum and Child, 1967; Marshall, 2001). Large protein complexes containing the precursor axoneme building blocks are delivered to this site via an evolutionary conserved process called intraflagellar transport (IFT; [Kozminski et al., 1993]). The roles of IFT in ciliary function are well studied (Pedersen and Rosenbaum, 2008), and the molecular mechanisms that mediate IFT of axonemal proteins are beginning to be characterized (Bhogaraju et al., 2013). The structure of the flagellar tip has been characterized; the B-tubule ends before the A-tubule creating a distal ‘singlet region’ in the flagellum tip of most species (Ringo, 1967; Satir, 1968; Sale and Satir, 1976; Woolley and Nickels, 1985); the CPs extend further into the distal tip than the dMTs (Ringo, 1967); the dMTs and CPs are linked to the membrane through capping structures (Dentler, 1980; Woolley et al., 2006). Yet, we know very little about how the flagellar components, once delivered to the distal tip, are assembled to form the beating flagellum (Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011; Fisch and Dupuis-Williams, 2012). For example, does the CP extend beyond the dMTs during tip growth, like in the mature flagellum, or is the growth of all MTs synchronized? Alternatively do the dMTs extend beyond the CP during flagellar extension? When do other structural modules such as radial spokes, dynein arms, and central pair projections get incorporated? Clearly, there are multiple possibilities for how a flagellum might extend.

We have examined two evolutionary distant organisms, the green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and the parasitic protozoa Trypanosoma brucei, to determine if a consistent pattern of flagellar extension exists. By studying the tips of their growing flagella and their basal plate region, we reveal two separate assembly pathways of flagella extension and maturation.

## Results

## Surprising microtubule arrangements at the flagellar tip

To elucidate the pathways for axoneme elongation, we used electron tomography to examine the tips of actively growing flagella in two organisms, just when the flagella have started growing (at ∼0.7–1.5 μm), and after a period of flagellar growth (at 4–10 μm; Table 1). C. reinhardtii has two flagella that are reabsorbed down to their transition zones, which are then expelled prior to mitosis (Rasi et al., 2009; Parker et al., 2010). After mitosis, the small daughter cells remain within the wall of the mother cell where they regrow their flagella; a cell stage we easily identified in the electron microscope. In T. brucei the new flagellum starts growing midway through the cell cycle (Sherwin and Gull, 1989). Its tip is attached to the side of the old flagellum by a structure called the flagella connector (Moreira-Leite, 2001; Briggs, 2004; Davidge, 2006). The relative positions of a cell’s two flagella allow an unambiguous identification of which flagellum is old and which is new (Figure 1A,B). Comparable images of new growing flagella that were short or long were also obtained from C. reinhardtii (Videos 4 and 5). The axoneme in all flagellar tips studied, except the T. brucei growing long flagella, displayed the regular spacing of dMTs found in the rest of the flagellum (Figure 1C,D,F,G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). In contrast, the growing long T. brucei flagellar tips showed a disorganized array of dMTs (Figure 1E); some dMTs lay very close to the CPs. The axoneme structure is revealed in 3D models of each of the tips (Figure 1C′–G′, Videos 6–10). We also investigated whether there was a difference between the elongation of CPs and dMTs. To show microtubule extension within the axoneme, we measured the distance from the ends of the A-, B-tubule and CP to the end of the furthest reaching microtubule of the axoneme. The ends of dMTs and CPs of flagellar ends did not significantly differ in their extension in most samples (Figure 3B; Table 3). However, we found a significant difference between the extensions of dMTs and CPs in the growing long T. brucei flagella, where the CP lagged behind the dMTs extension by approximately 50 nm (p<0.01). The small distance from the tip in which all the MT tips were found in both T. brucei and C. reinhardtii contradicts the existence of a long singlet region, previously published to be ∼1 μm in C. reinhardtii (Ringo, 1967; Satir, 1968; Sale and Satir, 1976; Woolley and Nickels, 1985). Furthermore, the extension of the A- and B-tubule within the dMTs revealed that the A-tubule commonly extended the furthest (Figure 3C). However, the extension of the longest sub-fiber did not protrude more than 10–20 nm beyond its partner tubule. No samples showed a significant difference between A- and B-tubule extension (Figure 3D; Table 3).

We also compared the distances from the MT ends to the tip membrane in high pressure frozen vs chemically fixed growing T. brucei flagella (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). In chemically fixed cells, the dMT and CP ends were found in a wide range of distances, up to 350 nm from the membrane (average 203 ± 75 nm; n = 40), in contrast to the high pressure frozen T. brucei flagella where the same distance was a maximum of 125 nm (45 ± 37 nm; n = 75). The microtubule plus ends within the same axoneme were spread over a larger distance in chemically fixed samples than in high pressure frozen ones. Indeed, a partial axoneme was previously used to localize an image as having been acquired close to the distal flagellum end (Briggs, 2004), when such an area of a partial axoneme was rarely to be found in this study. These findings, in combination with the absence of a singlet region in high-pressure frozen samples, indicate that the distal flagellar arrangements previously published in C. reinhardtii tips were likely disturbed by the chemical fixation used.

We conclude that the singlet region is not found in either species examined, but that the two species examined display two different assembly pathways.

Three cells were arranged by the lengths of their flagella and thus, their cell cycle stages (Figure 6C–E). The central cylinder looks like two stacked U’s in tomographic slices of all cells (Figure 6D). Density thresholding of our tomograms reveals that the U’s resemble two stacked baskets in 3D (Figure 6E). As the central cylinder grows, the proportions of the baskets remain surprisingly similar (Figure 6D,E), with the longer upper basket constituting 60 ± 5% of the total basal plate thickness and the more partial lower basket constituting 28 ± 5% (Figure 6F). Interestingly, in the one cell with long flagella where we reconstructed both transition zones, the two central cylinder structures were similar in thickness and in their anchoring of the CPs (Figure 6A,B; long flagellum).

We conclude that the structural alterations in the region of CP nucleation during flagellar maturation in T. brucei are not conserved between these two species, as the C. reinhardtii structure merely grows lengthwise.

Finally, we used this information to build a summarizing model of the two ways to grow and mature a flagellum in the protozoa T. brucei and C. reinhardtii. In T. brucei the growing axoneme is disorganized, with shorter CPs than dMTs, all of which are possibly not anchored to the flagellar membrane (Figure 7D). The associated axonemal protein modules such as radial spokes and CP projections are added in later assembly steps. In the proximal part of the growing flagellum, the basal plate is first arranged into two electron-dense rings close to which capped CP ends can be found. In the corresponding area of a mature flagellum, the basal plate is a loose electron-dense area in which one, sometimes two, open or closed CP minus ends are found.

In C. reinhardtii, the growing axoneme is not very different (on this ultrastructural level) from the mature axoneme as the circular arrangement, with the associated axonemal proteins, is maintained all the way to the growing tip (Figure 7E). This holds true also for the central structure of the transition zone, the only maturation of which seems to be a lengthwise extension.

## Discussion

Despite the remarkable conservation of the axonemal structure, we have shown two ways to build a flagellum; flagellar growth occurs in both species and length-dependent manner. Whereas, we see no difference in growth in short T. brucei and C. reinhardtii flagella, T. brucei long flagella appear to first elongate their axonemal MTs in a disordered manner, which is then stabilized to a circular arrangement by the addition of associated protein complexes such as the radial spokes. In contrast, our study suggests that the axonemal dMTs and structural proteins are assembling simultaneously in long C. reinhardtii. What regulates such differences in the assembly pathways? Dentler (1980) showed that the growing axoneme in C. reinhardtii had structures linking from the tips of the microtubules to the membrane. Woolley et al. (2006) failed to see such linking structures in growing flagella of Leishmania major (but did see them in mature flagella), a close relative to T. brucei. We speculate that the presence of such anchorage in C. reinhardtii could provide structural clues for the growing axoneme, holding it into a close-to-circular arrangement. This arrangement could then facilitate the incorporation of the associated axonemal proteins such as radial spokes.

Another explanation for the apparent difference in axonemal growth mechanism between T. brucei and C. reinhardtii could be that these flagella are elongating at different rates: snapshots of a fast-growing axoneme might capture disordered intermediates that are not seen in a more slowly elongating structure. However, the initial growth rate of regrowing C. reinhardtii flagella (shed by ionic shock) is approximately 12–24 µm/hr, which then declines to 9 µm/hr as the flagellum gets longer (Rosenbaum et al., 1969; Flavin and Slaughter, 1974). The growth rate of their flagella after mitosis remains unknown, but we assume equal or faster assembly because of the pre-mitotic reabsorbtion of the flagellar components that could then be utilized in the construction of the next flagellum. In T. brucei, we deduced the flagellum growth rate from the growth rate of the PFR to be a constant ∼4 µm/hr (Bastin et al., 1999). These growth rates indicate that the structural differences we see are not caused by a slower flagellar growth rate, and therefore more organized growth, in C. reinhardtii.

The differences in growth mechanics may not be so surprising, since the two species grow their flagella in different circumstances. In T. brucei, the new flagellum is not necessary for cell motility since the old flagellum is still present and active. In C. reinhardtii on the other hand, both flagella have been shed as a preparation for mitosis, so the cell is completely dependent on the reappearance of the two new flagella for its motility, making the rapid establishment of function important.

There are numerous further differences between the flagella of these two organisms: (1) The beat form of the flagella (Schmidt and Eckert, 1976; Heddergott et al., 2012). (2) The presence of a PFR in T. brucei (Vickerman, 1962; Bastin et al., 1998; Portman and Gull, 2010; Höög et al., 2012). (3) A rotational CP in C. reinhardtii; (Mitchell, 2003) vs a stationary CP T. brucei (Gadelha et al., 2006). Based on the findings presented in this paper, we can now add to this list a difference in the pathways for establishing axoneme organization during MT elongation, and maturation of the proximal region during the cell cycle.

It is important to note that we did not use deflagellation to create a situation of regenerating flagella in C. reinhardtii, as this regrowth might be different from the natural situation occurring when flagella regrow after mitosis. Pre-mitotic reabsorption of the flagellum probably allows for storage of the flagellar protein pool, a pool that would have been lost in the event of ionic shock deflagellation. Furthermore, in deflagellation before mitosis the basal plate is lost in a final event of shedding (Parker et al., 2010), whereas the stress induced deflagellation triggers a severing event distal to the basal plate, which can then form the transition zone for the next flagellum (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).

We also revealed that the flagellum tip structure might be different to what was previously described. Most notably, we found no evidence of a singlet region, which has been shown to be over 2 μm long in Tetrahymena sp (Sale and Satir, 1976) and ∼1 μm in C. reinhardtii. We also found no obvious CP cap, not disproving its existence (we did see evidence for filamentous proteins extending into the CP lumen), but showing that in well preserved cells it does not appear as previously described (Dentler and Rosenbaum, 1977; Dentler, 1980; Fisch and Dupuis-Williams, 2012). Even though we found the CPs to extend further than the dMTs, it was only within ∼50 nm, in contrast to the published flagellar tip arrangement in C. reinhardtii (of unknown dynamic state), that shows the central pair protruding ∼400 nm beyond the doublet microtubules (Ringo, 1967).

These differences in assembly order, speed, function, and structure, in two species both with the conventional 9+2 motile flagella structure, pose the question if the internal environments of flagella of different species are more different than presently assumed. Ciliogenesis will most likely involve a whole subset of flagellar proteins, with functions that are distinct from the IFT of axonemal proteins to the assembling tip. Flagellar growth rates after ionic shock in C. reinhardtii are length dependent, with shorter flagella growing faster than longer ones. Together with a steady disassembly rate, this forms the basis of the balance-point-model of flagellar length regulation (Marshall et al., 2005). The faster growth of short C. reinhardtii was then showed to depend on longer IFT trans in the short flagellum (Engel et al., 2009). This would fit well with our observations that the modes of assembly in the short and long post-mitotic C. reinhardtii tips do not differ beyond the point of central pair extension. Interestingly, we did detect differences in short vs long growing flagellar tips in T. brucei, an organism that most likely has linear flagellum growth. The absence of several axonemal components at the long growing tip might indicate that IFT is rate limiting in this growth. One would then predict that flagellar length is independent of size of IFT trains in these cells. However, it has recently been shown that the IFT traffic in T. brucei also differs considerably from that of C. reinhardtii (Buisson et al., 2013).

Thus, to further understand the normal structure and function of flagella, and the pathology of various ciliopathies, it is crucial to further understand ciliogenesis. With this paper we have revealed two modes of flagella growth, an area of flagellum biology that still remained mostly in the dark, and complementing our extensive knowledge on IFT of building material to the site of flagellar growth.

## Materials and methods

## Preparation T. brucei for electron tomography

Procyclic T. brucei strain 427 (high pressure freezing; HPF) or 29–13 (chemical fixation) were grown in SDM-79 media supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (for chemical fixation; PAA Laboratories Ltd, UK) and 20% fetal bovine serum (for HPF) (Brun and Schönenberger, 1979). Cell growth was monitored by using a CASY DT cell counter (Sedna Scientific, UK), and cultures were diluted on a daily basis to maintain a density between 5 × 105 and 1 × 107 cells per milliliter.

Cells were prepared for electron tomography by high pressure freezing or chemical fixation followed by epon embedding as described previously (Höög et al., 2010).

## Preparation of T. brucei for cryo-electron tomography

Unperturbed procyclic T. brucei strain 427 was plunge frozen and imaged intact as in (Höög et al., 2012).

## Preparation of C. reinhardtii for electron tomography

Wild-type Chlamydomonas reinhardtii strain 137C mt+ was grown at room temperature in liquid culture (Sagar and Granick medium) using a 10/14 dark/light cycle. After the cultures were shifted to the dark cycle, the cells were prepared for electron microscopy by HPF followed by freeze substitution as essentially described in O’Toole et al. (2003, 2007). Briefly, the liquid culture was spun at 500×g for 5 min and the loose pellet was resuspended in a medium containing 150 mM mannitol for 1 hr. The samples were then spun at 500×g, the supernatant decanted and the loose pellet frozen using a BAL-TEC HPM-010 high-pressure freezer. The frozen samples were freeze substituted in 1% OsO4 and 0.1% uranyl acetate in acetone for 3 days then embedded in epon/araldite resin.

## Serial sectioning and on-section staining

Semi-thick (300–400 nm) serial sections of the samples were cut using an ultracut UCT ultramicrotome (Leica Microsystems Ltd, UK). The sections were flattened by chloroform gas exposure whilst floating on the water surface. Ribbons of serial sections were put centered on 2 × 1 mm copper palladium slot grids (Agar Scientific Ltd, UK).

The sections were stained for 5 min on 2% uranyl acetate followed by 30 s Reynold’s lead citrate. 15-nm colloidal gold particles were applied to both sides of the grid, to be used for image alignment.

## Electron tomography and image analysis

Tilt series of serial sections from flagella distal tips were acquired using the serialEM software (Mastronarde, 2005) operating a Tecnai TF30 300 kV IVEM microscope (FEI Co., The Netherlands). Images were collected about two orthogonal axes in 1° increments (±60°) using a Gatan CCD camera (pixel size 0.76–1.3 nm). Tomographic reconstructions were calculated, the two axis combined, serial sections stitched together and models were created using the IMOD software package (Kremer et al., 1996; Mastronarde, 1997).

Note that not all flagella tips are complete within the reconstructed volume in one tomogram. Many are reconstructed over serial sections. Measurements were only done within the same tomogram to ensure no error was introduced in the joining process. All flagella visualized were followed through the serial sections, taking lower magnification images of the entire cell to be able to reconstruct the flagellum length. Microtubule ends were classified as in Höög et al. (2007, 2011, 2013).

results.result: The study reveals two distinct modes of flagellar assembly: in C. reinhardtii, microtubules and associated proteins are added simultaneously during growth, while in T. brucei, disorganized microtubules are first extended and then organized by later addition of preformed protein complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C11, C19-25, C56-67 provide converging electron tomography evidence showing organized growth in C. reinhardtii versus disorganized growth in T. brucei long flagella. The data from multiple flagellar stages, quantitative measurements, and visual evidence from Figures 1-2 and 7 strongly support this major finding.

results.result: Growing long T. brucei flagellar tips show disorganized doublet microtubules lacking associated structural proteins like central pair projections, suggesting microtubules extend beyond where associated proteins are positioned.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-25 are supported by electron tomography data in Figures 1E and 2G showing disorganized dMTs and absence of structural proteins at growing tips. The inference that microtubules extend beyond associated proteins (C24-25) is reasonable given the visual evidence, though the sample size is relatively small (n=10 long flagella per Table 1).

results.result: Quantitative analysis reveals species-specific differences in microtubule extension patterns: in T. brucei long flagella, central pairs lag behind doublet microtubules by ~50 nm, while in C. reinhardtii, central pairs extend ~50 nm beyond doublet microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-31 are supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3 and Tables 2-3, with statistical testing (p<0.01 for differences). The measurements are precise and the sample sizes adequate (n=47-97 microtubules per condition). The finding that A- and B-tubule extension differs by only 10-20 nm challenges previous models of singlet regions.

results.result: High-pressure frozen samples show no evidence of the previously reported singlet region in either species, with microtubule ends within 125 nm of the membrane, suggesting that chemical fixation artifacts distorted previous observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-35 are well-supported by comparative data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing dramatic differences between chemical fixation (up to 350 nm) and high-pressure freezing (max 125 nm). The conclusion that previous singlet region observations were fixation artifacts is reasonable, though the authors appropriately note they cannot completely disprove the existence of CP caps (C88).

results.result: The T. brucei basal plate undergoes structural maturation during the cell cycle, transitioning from a defined two-ring structure with capped central pair minus ends in new flagella to a diffuse electron-dense mass with loosened central pair anchoring in old flagella.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-49 are supported by detailed electron tomography reconstructions of 10 flagella across 5 cells at different cell cycle stages (Figure 5). The progression from organized two-ring structure (~30 nm) to diffuse mass (up to 90 nm) is well-documented visually and quantitatively. The observation of capped ends in new flagella (4/4) versus open ends in old flagella (6/9) provides strong evidence for maturation.

results.result: The C. reinhardtii transition zone central cylinder consists of two stacked baskets that maintain consistent proportions (upper basket 60±5%, lower basket 28±5%) as the structure grows lengthwise, showing no structural alterations comparable to T. brucei maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-55 are supported by electron tomography data from 9 transition zones (Figure 6). The quantitative analysis showing consistent proportions despite size variation is convincing. The conclusion that maturation differs between species (C54) is well-supported by the comparative data, though the sample size for C. reinhardtii is smaller than for T. brucei.

results.result: Flagellar growth is length-dependent in both species, with no differences observed in short flagella between species, but distinct assembly mechanisms emerging in long flagella where T. brucei shows disorganized growth while C. reinhardtii maintains organized simultaneous assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-67, C96-97 are supported by comparative electron tomography data across different flagellar lengths. The observation that short flagella show similar assembly in both species while long flagella differ is well-documented in Figures 1-2 and 7. The inference about simultaneous vs. sequential assembly is reasonable given the structural evidence.

results.result: Growth rate analysis shows C. reinhardtii flagella initially grow at 12-24 μm/hr (declining to 9 μm/hr) while T. brucei flagella grow at a constant ~4 μm/hr, indicating that the observed structural differences are not due to slower growth in C. reinhardtii.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-74 are supported by citations to prior work for C. reinhardtii growth rates and inference from PFR growth data for T. brucei. The logic that faster growth in C. reinhardtii rules out growth rate as an explanation for more organized assembly is sound. However, C73 involves indirect inference from PFR data rather than direct measurement.

results.result: The presence of membrane-linking structures in C. reinhardtii (but not in Leishmania major, a T. brucei relative) may provide structural guidance that maintains circular arrangement and facilitates incorporation of associated proteins during growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-69 cite prior work, but C70-71 are explicitly speculative ("We speculate," "could facilitate"). While the hypothesis is reasonable given the observed differences, the authors provide no direct evidence for membrane-linking structures in their own data. This remains an untested mechanistic explanation requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: The different cellular contexts for flagellar growth—T. brucei retains a functional old flagellum during new flagellum growth while C. reinhardtii depends entirely on rapid regrowth of both flagella after mitosis—may explain the different assembly strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-77 are based on established knowledge of the cell biology of both organisms. The inference that functional requirements influence assembly strategy is reasonable, though this represents interpretation rather than direct experimental evidence. The logic connecting cellular context to assembly mechanism is plausible but not experimentally tested in this study.

results.result: Electron tomography reveals both flared and capped microtubule ends in growing flagella, with electron-dense structures associated with central pairs and A-tubules extending into microtubule lumens in mature flagella.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-40 are supported by visual evidence in Figure 4, showing different microtubule end morphologies and electron-dense structures. The observations are descriptive and well-documented through both conventional and cryo-electron tomography. These structural details support the broader assembly mechanism findings.

results.result: The study used post-mitotic flagellar regrowth rather than deflagellation-induced regrowth in C. reinhardtii because these processes differ in protein pool availability and basal plate retention, potentially affecting assembly mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-87 explain important methodological choices. C82 is a factual statement about methods, while C83-87 provide reasonable justification based on cited literature (C86-87) and biological reasoning (C83-85). This methodological consideration strengthens the study by using more physiologically relevant conditions, though C83 acknowledges uncertainty about potential differences.

results.result: Well-preserved cells show no obvious central pair cap structure and central pairs extend only ~50 nm beyond doublet microtubules, contrasting with previous reports of ~400 nm protrusion in C. reinhardtii.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-90 are supported by electron tomography data and comparison with prior literature (Ringo, 1967). The authors appropriately note they cannot disprove CP cap existence but show it doesn't appear as previously described. The discrepancy with prior work is likely explained by fixation artifacts (C32-34), making this a valid correction to the literature.

results.result: The observed differences in assembly order, speed, function, and structure between two species with conventional 9+2 flagella suggest that flagellar internal environments may be more species-specific than currently assumed, with ciliogenesis likely involving distinct protein subsets beyond IFT machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-92 represent broader implications drawn from the comparative data. C91 is a reasonable inference from the documented differences, while C92 is explicitly speculative ("will most likely"). These claims appropriately frame the significance of the findings for understanding flagellar diversity and complexity, though they call for future work rather than providing direct evidence.

results.result: Length-dependent growth rates in C. reinhardtii, which form the basis of the balance-point model of flagellar length regulation and depend on IFT train length, are consistent with the observation that assembly modes in short versus long post-mitotic C. reinhardtii flagella do not differ beyond central pair extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-95 cite established prior work on length regulation mechanisms. C96 connects this prior knowledge to the current observations, showing internal consistency. The integration of prior models with new structural data is appropriate, though this represents interpretation of how current findings fit existing frameworks rather than new experimental evidence.

results.result: T. brucei likely has linear flagellum growth, and the absence of axonemal components at long growing tips might indicate IFT rate limitation, though IFT traffic in T. brucei differs considerably from C. reinhardtii.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-100 are explicitly speculative ("most likely," "might indicate," "would predict"). While C101 cites recent work showing IFT differences, the mechanistic explanations in C99-100 are hypotheses requiring experimental testing. The speculation is reasonable but represents future work rather than supported conclusions from the current data.

results.result: Defects in cilia and flagella cause various human ciliopathies including primary ciliary dyskinesia, which are diagnosed by ultrastructural investigations, making species-specific structural knowledge critical for evaluating flagellar defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-3 cite established medical literature on ciliopathies. C14 represents the authors' conclusion about the clinical relevance of their findings. While the connection between the comparative structural biology and clinical diagnosis is somewhat indirect, the logic that understanding normal species-specific assembly is important for interpreting pathology is sound.

results.result: Flagella consist of ~1000 proteins that are delivered via intraflagellar transport to the distal end where they assemble, with previous work showing B-tubules end before A-tubules creating singlet regions, central pairs extending beyond doublets, and capping structures linking microtubules to membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-9 summarize established background knowledge from cited literature. These claims provide context for the study but are not novel findings. Notably, the current study challenges some of these prior observations (particularly C7 about singlet regions), which the authors appropriately address in their results.

results.result: C. reinhardtii reabsorbs and expels flagella before mitosis then regrows them in daughter cells, while T. brucei grows a new flagellum attached to the old flagellum via a flagella connector midway through the cell cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-18 describe the cell biological context for each organism based on cited literature and established knowledge. These factual descriptions of the experimental systems are well-supported and essential for interpreting the assembly observations, though they represent background rather than novel findings.

results.result: T. brucei and C. reinhardtii flagella differ in beat form, presence of paraflagellar rod structure (T. brucei only), and central pair behavior (rotational in C. reinhardtii, stationary in T. brucei).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-81 cite prior literature documenting structural and functional differences between the two species. These established differences provide important context for understanding why assembly mechanisms might differ, though they are not novel findings from this study.

results.result: The manuscript claims that C. reinhardtii and T. brucei use two fundamentally different mechanisms/pathways for flagellar assembly: simultaneous addition of microtubules and associated proteins in C. reinhardtii versus sequential assembly (disorganized microtubules followed by protein complex addition) in T. brucei.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the study 'intriguing' and liked 'the idea that there are different modes of assembly,' but expressed the main concern that 'you are over-stating your case. It may be that you are seeing different mechanisms, but you could easily be looking at different kinetics.' They recommend calling them 'different modes of assembly, rather than different mechanisms' and discussing alternative interpretations including how delayed protein incorporation may affect assembly kinetics.

results.result: In T. brucei long flagella, the growing tip shows disorganized doublet microtubules (dMTs) with absent associated protein complexes (radial spokes, central pair projections), suggesting microtubules extend beyond associated proteins which are added later to stabilize the axoneme structure.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accepted the observations, they raised concerns about interpretation, suggesting that 'the delayed incorporation of structural proteins that cross-link (and thus likely stabilize) the axonemal MTs may result in a less stable tip, which would in turn affect the kinetics of flagellar assembly.' This indicates the data could reflect kinetic differences rather than fundamentally different mechanisms.

results.result: In C. reinhardtii, the growing axoneme maintains circular arrangement with associated axonemal proteins present all the way to the growing tip, suggesting simultaneous assembly of microtubules and structural proteins.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the observations but questioned whether this represents a different mechanism versus different kinetics. They suggested the authors 'discuss other ways of interpreting your data' and consider how the presence of stabilizing proteins might affect assembly kinetics rather than representing a fundamentally different assembly pathway.

results.result: Quantitative measurements show species-specific differences in microtubule-to-membrane distances and relative extension of central pairs versus doublet microtubules, with T. brucei showing microtubules touching the membrane in long new flagella and CPs lagging behind dMTs, while C. reinhardtii shows CPs extending further than dMTs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these quantitative observations directly. However, they noted that 'given that you only have 5 tomograms per condition, the data set is a bit limited, and that you should state this caveat somewhere,' indicating acceptance of the findings with acknowledgment of sample size limitations.

results.result: High-pressure freezing reveals that previously reported flagellar tip structures (singlet region, extensive CP protrusion) in C. reinhardtii were likely artifacts of chemical fixation, as high-pressure frozen samples show no singlet region and only ~50 nm CP extension beyond dMTs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these methodological findings about fixation artifacts. The observations about preservation quality and differences between fixation methods appear to be accepted as valid technical contributions.

results.result: The T. brucei transition zone basal plate undergoes structural maturation during flagellar growth, changing from two stacked electron-dense rings (~30 nm thick) with capped CP minus ends in new flagella to a diffuse electron-dense mass (up to 90 nm thick) with open CP ends in old flagella.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these structural observations of the transition zone. The detailed characterization of basal plate maturation appears to be accepted as a valid finding.

results.result: The C. reinhardtii transition zone central cylinder consists of two stacked baskets that maintain consistent proportions (60±5% upper, 28±5% lower) as they grow lengthwise during maturation, contrasting with the structural alterations seen in T. brucei.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these structural observations about the C. reinhardtii transition zone. The characterization of the basket structure and its growth pattern appears to be accepted.

results.result: Flagellar growth occurs in a length-dependent manner in both species, with no differences detected between short T. brucei and C. reinhardtii flagella, but differences appearing in long growing flagellar tips of T. brucei.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these observations about length-dependent differences. The finding that short flagella are similar while long flagella differ appears to be accepted as valid.

results.result: The study used post-mitotic flagellar regrowth rather than pH shock-induced deflagellation for C. reinhardtii, as these represent different biological situations with different protein pools and basal plate retention.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly requested that authors 'comment on why you did not use regeneration after pH shock, as this is a standard way to look at growth.' This indicates concern about the methodological choice and whether it affects interpretation of the results.

results.result: C. reinhardtii daughter cells remain within the mother cell wall where they regrow flagella after mitosis, ensuring the observed flagella are in a growing state.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted 'we realised that because they are always within the mother wall, this means that they must be growing, but you should make this point explicit in the text,' indicating acceptance of this reasoning once clarified.

results.result: Growth rate comparisons show C. reinhardtii flagella initially grow at 12-24 μm/hr (declining to 9 μm/hr) while T. brucei grows at constant ~4 μm/hr, indicating structural differences are not due to slower growth in C. reinhardtii.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these growth rate comparisons or the inference that structural differences are not simply due to growth speed differences. This reasoning appears to be accepted.

results.result: Electron tomography reveals both flared and capped microtubule ends in flagellar tips, with electron-dense structures associated with central pairs and electron density extending into microtubule lumens in mature T. brucei flagella.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these detailed structural observations from electron tomography. These appear to be accepted as valid descriptive findings.

results.result: Defects in cilia and flagella cause various human ciliopathies, and species-specific structural knowledge is critical before evaluating flagellar defects, providing medical relevance for understanding different assembly mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted they 'like...the potential link to the structures seen in PCD patients,' indicating acceptance of the medical relevance and the importance of understanding species-specific differences for clinical applications.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the main finding about organized vs. disorganized growth (C10, C11, C13, C36, C63, C102). OpenEval finds the evidence strongly supportive, while peer reviewers accept the observations but express concern about overstating the case, suggesting the differences may reflect kinetics rather than fundamentally different mechanisms.

Both address disorganized dMTs and protein incorporation in T. brucei long flagella (C19-C25). OpenEval finds the electron tomography data supportive with reasonable inferences. Peer reviewers accept the observations but question interpretation, suggesting delayed protein incorporation may affect assembly kinetics rather than representing a different mechanism.

Both evaluate quantitative measurements of A- and B-tubule extension differences (C26-C31). OpenEval finds the data well-supported with adequate statistical testing and sample sizes. Peer reviewers accept the findings but note the limited dataset (5 tomograms per condition) and request this caveat be stated.
